messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Salesperson
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Frank was a 70-year-old North American man who had worked for years as a salesperson and was still trying to keep up the routines that gave shape to his days. By the time he first came to treatment, he was married and living with a sense that something in him had shifted in a way he could not quite explain to his wife or to himself. The event he kept returning to had happened in a public place he had no choice but to pass in the course of ordinary life. One evening, he had been confronted and assaulted by a man he understood as the offender, and the encounter had been so abrupt and so humiliating that, even months later, he could still summon it in fragments: the offender’s face close enough to study, the sudden aggression, the sharp bodily alarm, and the smell of alcohol hanging around the man. That smell had become one of the clearest pieces of the memory for Frank, not because he sought it out, but because it seemed to bring the whole scene back with a force that left him feeling as if he were there again.

In the weeks after the assault, Frank began having unwanted thoughts that arrived without warning while he was doing ordinary things. He might be talking with a customer, driving, or sitting at the kitchen table with his wife when the scene would intrude and he would find himself back in that moment, not by choice but with a kind of grim certainty that it could happen again. What frightened him most was how specific these moments felt when they came: if he caught the smell of alcohol in a restaurant or on someone passing by, he would tense immediately, scanning the room before he could even tell himself to relax. He also became sharply alert to any resemblance to the offender’s face. Once, while working, he saw a man whose features were enough like the attacker’s that Frank had to look away and steady himself before he could continue the conversation. He did not tell the customer why he had suddenly gone quiet; he simply tried to regain control and move on as though nothing had happened.

As time went on, Frank started changing the places he would go. He began avoiding the location where the assault had happened, and then, gradually, anywhere near it. If a sales route or errand would have taken him close to that area, he found reasons to alter it. He told himself it was practical, that there was no sense in putting himself in a situation that made him feel unsettled, but the pattern narrowed his world in ways his wife noticed before he was willing to name them. He no longer lingered in parts of town he used to move through without thinking. Even when his work required him to stay active and visible, he organized his days so that he would not have to come near the place that held the memory. The change was especially hard because his occupation depended on being comfortable with people and locations he did not control, and now each outing could become a calculation about whether he might encounter the wrong smell, the wrong face, or the wrong street.

At home, Frank had come to believe that the person he had become was unrecognisable to him. He described himself as someone who had grown flat and distant, and he said there was something wrong with him as a person because he no longer responded to life the way he used to. He spoke with particular pain about the way he blamed himself for what happened, convinced that the event had occurred because of the way he acted. He replayed his own behavior in the encounter and kept arriving at the same conclusion: if he had said something differently, stood differently, moved faster, or simply not been there in that moment, things might have turned out otherwise. These thoughts sat beside the more immediate habit of trying not to think about the trauma. When the memory surfaced, he would push it away, change the subject, or immerse himself in something else, and he described numbness as the safest way to get through the day. He said he was trying hard not to think about it, because once he let himself start, it seemed to spread through everything.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become hard to ignore. His wife could see that he was more distant, less himself, and Frank was tired of living around his own alarm and avoidance. He came in not because he felt ready to revisit the assault, but because he could no longer keep arranging his life around it without noticing the cost. What he most feared was that the change in him was permanent, that he had somehow become the damaged version of himself he now saw in the mirror. At the same time, he was hoping that talking might help him understand why one assault had left such a lasting mark, and whether there was any way to feel like his own person again.
